 QQQ is the fund that holds the AI leaders. Say you put $1 million into it on Nov 18, 2021. You reinvested every dividend and never sold. At Wednesday's close, it was worth about $1.69 million . 
 That is the ending. The path to it was much harder. 
 How Far Did $1 Million In QQQ Fall? 
 It sat below $1 million for almost two years. 
 Six weeks after you bought, it started falling. By Nov 3, 2022, your million was worth $652,000 . From January 2022, it stayed below what you paid for 487 trading days in a row. That is about 23 months. It did not get back above $1 million for good until Dec 12, 2023. 
 To get from $652,000 back to $1 million, QQQ needed a 53% gain. It got one, rising 54.9% in 2023. But nobody knew that in November 2022. 
 The swings have not stopped. On Oct 6, the same million was worth $1.95 million. Six weeks later, at the Nov 18 close, it was $1.69 million. That is $257,000 less. Across the whole five years, it was below $1 million on 41% of all trading days. 
 QQQ's million fell to $652,000 before it grew to $1.69 million. Growth is easier to hold on to when the rest of your money falls less. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3x the S&P 500's, and it lost less than the S&P 500 in all 9 big selloffs since 2018. See the metrics .

 Source: Trefis, prices through Nov 18. $1 million invested Nov 18, 2021, with dividends reinvested. The columns show the value at the Nov 18, 2026 close, the lowest value along the way, and the longest unbroken run of trading days below $1 million (21 trading days to a month). 
 Look at the first three rows. QQQ, the S&P 500 and the dividend fund SCHD all ended within $110,000 of each other. Their paths were very different. QQQ spent 23 months below $1 million, and SCHD spent four. Their worst points were $221,000 apart. We looked at SCHD on its own in $1 Million In SCHD Five Years Ago: What Is It Worth Now? 
 What If A Fund Never Gets Back? 
 It happens. 
 ARKK is an innovation fund that rose 153% in 2020. It then turned $1 million into $263,000 by December 2022. It rose 69% in 2023, 8% in 2024 and 35% in 2025. That is three good years in a row. Yet at Wednesday's close, the million was still only $635,000. In five years, it never once closed back above $1 million. From $263,000, it needed to almost quadruple. From here, it still needs a 58% gain. 
 Story Continues The chip fund SMH shows the other side. Its $1 million became $3.05 million. But first it fell to $561,000. And it is down 31% since June, which is $1.39 million gone in five months. A single stock, Nvidia , went through the same thing on a larger scale. 
 So Which Number Should You Look At? 
 The worst one. 
 Before you buy a fund, look at its worst point and its longest time below what you paid. Do not look only at the ending. Then ask yourself an honest question. At $652,000, 11 months in, would I still hold? 
 If the answer is no, the fund that ended highest is not the right one for you. The right one is the fund whose bad years you can sit through. In our view, the AI leaders work best as part of a plan, not the whole plan. They can sit beside companies that pay you while you wait. 
 Some people would rather wait it out in cash. We show what waiting paid in $1 Million In Cash Five Years Ago: What Is It Worth Now? 
 The point to remember: $1 million in QQQ became $1.69 million, but only after 23 months below $1 million. Judge a fund by its worst years, not just its ending. The worst years decide whether you are still invested when the good ones come. 
 How big a fall you can sit through depends on your own life, such as when you plan to retire. A decision that big is worth planning before the next fall, not during it.
